title: AI isn’t killing creativity. It’s just letting us try ideas faster.
author: Santiago_Lawliet
selftext:
Wrote an article about the anti AI sentiment.   
What do you all think about it ?

comments.author: Drakim
comments.body:
I agree with your overall point, as fast iteration is actually really good for great game design. Fast iteration allows you to try things out, how they feel, what works and what doesn't work, without a huge investment.

It is often the reason people put scripting engines into their games so they don't have to recompile and restart the entire game to make rapid changes.

However, like the butterfly effect, there is no change that only has one consequence. I've seen a lot of AI games that are complete garbage, especially with those platforms that rapidly allows you to church out a game from a short description. This isn't because of AI, but because the barrier to entry has significantly lowered. The further back in time you go, the more difficult it was to make a game, and thus the more thoughts, reflections, blood, sweat and tears was put into it. When you can make the game at the push of a button, a lot of people are just gonna push that button and call it an day, and the game is gonna be bad and boring.

My advice is to not use AI as an excuse not to sharpen your skills. If you don't bother learning to code because the AI can just handle the coding for you, that mindset is going to undermine you as you won't put effort into other things either.

replies.author: tomByrer
replies.body:
\> AI games that are complete garbage

Oh, there are many games before AI that are also garbage.  & sometimes garbage games are fun, as long as you know they are before trying.

While I agree with both of you, I don't like how OP is really advertising his platform disguised as an 'article'.

replies.author: imnotabot303
replies.body:
That's pretty much all this sub is, 99% of it is just self promotion and people posting their AI gen games which are nearly always just clones anyway, and a bunch of ads for paid AI tool platforms, usually aimed at people who know nothing about game dev.

I think the majority of people here are either people wanting to churn out easy mode low effort games or AI "tech bro" types that think they are going to get rich quick with their new subscription AI service.

replies.author: d-czar
replies.body: I would add that AI is a great way to help you learn skills — not a substitute for them but an education amplified if you use it right, because it can explain everything, help you create working examples, etc. It’s amazing for learning — i feel like people overlook this in the debates about vibe coding vs real coding.

replies.author: Drakim
replies.body:
I super agree!
But learning skills takes effort, AI is just a tool that helps you learn better and faster, but it still takes effort. AI is also a tool that can do things for you so that you don't need to learn skills to gets results. The danger is leaning too much in that direction, hindering your own growth.

replies.author: Suatae
replies.body: The main problems that have always existed and that AI has put a highlight on are "laziness" and a "quick buck". People just want to make more money with the least amount of effort. It was asset flip clone games and now it's AI slop games. I doubt that there will ever be an end to them.

replies.author: Varrianda
replies.body:
If you can’t code, I don’t see a world where you can successfully build a large and good game. I’m a software engineer professionally, and have 15 years total experience. I’ve never made a game before, but I’ve designed a lot of systems.

I have some pretty strict rules as I’m making an MMO. Everything must be completely decoupled, no systems know of the existence of any other system. Everything is explicitly server authoritative except animation and visuals. Everything must be built to follow my architecture(it’s essentially just a fancy state machine). When building the game originally, everything was built knowing it would eventually be toggled to be netcode based. UI must only act as a display for information from the server and can not fetch any of that information itself.

The codebase has gotten massive and feature delivery has slowed down quite a bit, but even with my strict rules, it still sometimes tries to skip the server authority or tries to couple systems together. I spent a lot of time planning this architecture too. I just can’t imagine how someone with no coding experience(and, imo what’s more important now, architecture experience) can really make use of cibe coding. It’s just not there yet.

replies.author: Suatae
replies.body: My thoughts exactly. I'm currently making a game. It's slow going as a solo dev but that's because I want to learn and grow and refine my skills as I go. In the meantime I'm using AI to help me envision what my game would look like. I ask for coding help as well as help me understand it's coding answers. And at the same time I'm learning how to code and how to think as a coder. I tell this to people and the main response have been ridicule.

replies.author: Santiago_Lawliet
replies.body: All the best to both of you, and yeah this is what I am talking about if we are looking at a bigger picture even keeping the creative perspective- you got to learn how to build it right.

replies.author: Santiago_Lawliet
replies.body:
Completely agree, and it shouldn’t be used as an excuse but it could also help those people who want to just test out and get going, because those who want to learn will definitely learn. 

It’s all about keeping all sorts of options on the table.

comments.author: atx78701
comments.body:
people are being emotional about it and incredibly hostile. AI is a miracle tool and has increased my game dev productivity dramatically. 

You can look at john henry vs the steam locomotive to see that the arguments arent new at all.

Every new technology took jobs, but in the end our jobs are safer than ever, we are more productive, and people are still pretty much fully employed.

Look at tiktok/youtube etc, it allowed anyone to push media into the news or for entertainment. Millions of people became ministars outside the purview of hollywood or the legacy media. All those tools were not AI but they enabled everyday people to create content.

Low code tools, libraries etc did that for building software. 25 years ago it cost millions to build software. Then the tools like wordpress/wix/magento/shopify got better and better so anyone can deploy/build certain types of software

Then low code came up and let people deploy software faster than ever. Now AI is doing it 10x faster than lowcode.

You can fight it or you can adopt it.

replies.author: fjaoaoaoao
replies.body:
You can also do both, doesn’t have to be a false dichotomy.

Truly AI can be a boon but regulation is also needed and culture needs to adapt productively, not destructively. Like another poster alluded to, people need to use AI to enhance their capabilities, to sharpen their thinking and raise the standard, not lower the standard while people get hurt.

replies.author: Santiago_Lawliet
replies.body: exactly my point. Well articulated though.

comments.author: superkickstart
comments.body: The real problem is executives and people who think they can replicate in one shot and with minimal effort, what skilled people produce through experience. The result is just cheap useless slop, and when that kind of content dominates, it can turn and will turn people against AI. AI is a powerful tool and a productivity multiplier, but it only works if you already know your stuff, understand how to use AI tools correctly and and know how to integrate it into an existing workflow.

comments.author: DangiGuerrillaFlow_
comments.body:
Some people are unable to touch game development, and they can now explore this frontier thanks to AI.  I am one of those. I think you will get to see crazy gameideas in the future because of new people from different fields will be able to come up with unique ideas in game design.

For me, English has become a programming language because of AI.

I’m a traditional animator. I’ve seen AI in my field eating into commercial animation jobs. At first, I was completely against it. But slowly I realised the world isn’t going to stop for any of us.

Production managers—especially in my region—are already turning to AI for fast, high-volume work. I’m not talking about filmmaking, but commercial and short-format animation. As a result, many small animators are becoming jobless.

On the other hand, if you’re creative enough to tell a strong story and you understand animation deeply, you can still stand out in the AI noise. Skill plus vision matters more than ever.

replies.author: Santiago_Lawliet
replies.body: exactly now atleast a big chunk of people who may have never given it a shot, are now trying to create. That’s a silver lining right there.

comments.author: Constant_Physics8504
comments.body: Actually, it is half-and-half. You are correct, because you’re looking at it from the perspective of the developer, however, from the perspective of the consumer, when you put in a prompt, even if you’re prompt is unique, the game that gets developed has a strong similarity to other games being developed by the same platform. The reasoning is while your concept may be unique, the patterns, text stack, UI generation are not.

comments.author: Objective-Address810
comments.body:
Oh totally agree. I once went into a popular game dev reddit naïve in full of ideas and they bombed me into oblivion.

6 months later I have a production preview site, much of my backed  gameplay infrastructure solid, and plenty of milestones left to achieve.

AI made certain things more accessible for me, in order for me to experiment with ideas that were not previously possible.  


I have a tech background but not game dev. I have a lot of gameplay experience, but have never made a game. AI let me tap into that.
